lesson.title: assert: Programmer Sanity Checks, Not User Input Guards
lesson.summary: The assert statement raises an AssertionError when a condition it checks turns out false, and it exists to catch impossible states during development and testing, not to validate untrusted input in a finished program.
lesson.body:
You already have a general sense of what an assertion is and why unit testing matters: a test compares what your code actually produced against what it should have produced, and flags a failure the moment those two disagree. assert is the concrete piece of Python syntax that makes that comparison happen. Written as assert condition, optional_message, it evaluates condition, and if that condition is truthy, execution continues as if nothing happened. If the condition is falsy, Python immediately raises an AssertionError, using optional_message as the error's text if you supplied one.

```python
def average(numbers):
    assert len(numbers) > 0, "average() requires at least one number"
    return sum(numbers) / len(numbers)

print(average([10, 20, 30]))
average([])
```

average([10, 20, 30]) passes the assertion, since len(numbers) is 3, which is greater than 0, so execution continues to sum(numbers) / len(numbers), which is 60 divided by 3, or 20.0. average([]) fails it immediately, len([]) is 0, so the condition len(numbers) > 0 is False, and Python raises an AssertionError carrying the message before the division by zero that would otherwise occur ever gets a chance to run. The output is:

```
20.0
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
AssertionError: average() requires at least one number
```

with the program halting at that unhandled exception. There is an important line to draw around when to use assert, though. Assertions are meant to catch conditions that should be logically impossible if your own code is correct, things you use while developing and testing to document and verify your own assumptions, essentially a note to yourself that says this should never happen, and if it does, something in my own logic is broken. They are not meant to validate input coming from outside your program, from a user, a file, a network request, because Python can be run with the -O optimize flag, which strips out every assert statement in the entire program as if it were never written. Code that depends on an assert to reject bad user input would silently stop rejecting anything the moment someone runs it with -O, letting invalid data flow straight through. For anything that must always be checked, no matter how the program is run, raise an explicit exception instead, something like if len(numbers) == 0: raise ValueError("numbers cannot be empty"), since raise statements are never optimized away. assert is for programmer sanity checks and test code; raise is for guarding against real-world input.
